concepts.name: Constitutional Basis of Pardoning Power — Article 72
key_dimensions: Exact text and scope of Article 72 vs. Article 161 (Governor's power)
Nature of power: executive vs. quasi-judicial vs. constitutional discretion
Whether pardoning power is part of basic structure of Constitution
Distinction between Article 72 as a constitutional right of the convict vs. a privilege granted by the President

concepts.name: Five Forms of Clemency under Article 72
key_dimensions: Precise definitions: Pardon, Reprieve, Respite, Remission, Commutation — distinguishing each
UPSC trap: which forms reduce the sentence vs. which suspend vs. which replace with a lesser punishment
Pardon as the only form that completely absolves the convict — legal effect on civil disabilities
Reprieve vs. Respite: temporary suspension — when each is applicable (e.g., pregnant woman → Respite)

concepts.name: Exclusive Jurisdiction of President vs. Governor — Comparative Scope
key_dimensions: Cases where ONLY the President can pardon: court-martial sentences, death sentences, offences against Union law
Governor cannot pardon death sentences — only President can (Article 161 limitation)
Overlap scenario: offence punishable under both State and Union law — who has jurisdiction?
UPSC trap: Governor can suspend/remit/commute death sentences but CANNOT pardon them

concepts.name: Pardoning Power in Court-Martial Cases
key_dimensions: Exclusive presidential power — Governor has NO analogous power for court-martial
Constitutional provision: Article 72(1)(a) — sentences or punishments by court-martial
Practical significance: military personnel exclusively under President's clemency jurisdiction
Distinction between court-martial pardons and civilian criminal pardons under Article 72

concepts.name: Death Sentence and Presidential Pardon — Special Significance
key_dimensions: Article 72(1)(c): President's exclusive power to grant pardon/commutation in death sentence cases
Judicial scrutiny: Epuru Sudhakar case (2006) — death sentence pardons subject to judicial review on limited grounds
Delay in disposal of mercy petitions as a ground for commutation — Sher Singh vs. State of Punjab, Triveniben case
Right of convict to be heard / procedural aspects: whether natural justice applies

concepts.name: Binding Nature of Ministerial Advice on Pardoning Power
key_dimensions: Article 74(1): President SHALL act on aid and advice of Council of Ministers — applicability to pardoning power
44th Constitutional Amendment: President can send advice back once for reconsideration, but must act on re-submitted advice
Maru Ram vs. Union of India (1981): settled that President exercises pardoning power on advice of Cabinet, NOT independently
Tension between constitutional design (individual justice) and political executive advice — debates and criticism

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Pardoning Power
key_dimensions: Pardoning power NOT absolute — subject to judicial review on grounds of arbitrariness, mala fide, non-application of mind
Kehar Singh vs. Union of India (1989): SC held President need not give reasons; court cannot examine merits of decision
Epuru Sudhakar vs. Govt. of AP (2006): expanded scope of review — political consideration is a vitiating factor
Grounds on which courts WILL intervene vs. grounds on which they WON'T — the narrow window of reviewability

concepts.name: Non-Justiciability vs. Reviewability Paradox
key_dimensions: Historical position: pardoning power as sovereign/prerogative power beyond judicial reach
Shift in jurisprudence: from Maru Ram to Epuru Sudhakar — widening judicial oversight
Grounds explicitly excluded from review: President not required to hear the convict, no obligation to give reasons
UPSC trap: 'not subject to judicial review' is INCORRECT — it IS subject to review on LIMITED grounds

concepts.name: Delay in Mercy Petition Disposal as a Constitutional Issue
key_dimensions: Prolonged delay in deciding mercy petitions as cruel and unusual punishment — violation of Article 21
Landmark cases: Triveniben (1989), Shatrughan Chauhan vs. Union of India (2014) — delay can be ground for commutation
What constitutes 'undue delay' — no fixed timeline prescribed constitutionally
Procedural safeguards mandated by SC: solitary confinement during delay is unconstitutional

concepts.name: Pardoning Power and Offences Under Union vs. State Law
key_dimensions: Article 72 applies to: (a) court-martial, (b) Union law offences, (c) death sentences
Article 161 applies to: offences against State laws — Governor's domain
Critical grey area: IPC offences — investigated by State police but IPC is Union law (Entry 1, List III)
Supreme Court on IPC offences: both President and Governor may have concurrent pardoning jurisdiction — UPSC favourite trap

concepts.name: Remission vs. Commutation — Legal and Practical Distinction
key_dimensions: Remission: reduces quantum/duration of punishment WITHOUT changing its character (e.g., 10 years reduced to 5)
Commutation: substitutes one form of punishment for a lighter form (e.g., death → life imprisonment)
UPSC trap: Remission does NOT change the nature of punishment; Commutation DOES change the nature
Effect on civil rights and disqualifications: Remission vs. full Pardon — pardon alone removes all legal disabilities

concepts.name: Reprieve — Temporary Suspension of Punishment
key_dimensions: Definition: temporary suspension of sentence to allow convict to seek higher court relief or other remedy
Distinguished from Respite: Reprieve is temporary stay; Respite awards a lesser sentence on special grounds
Typical use cases: stay of execution pending a mercy petition review
Judicial interpretation: whether reprieve can be indefinitely extended — implications for death row convicts

concepts.name: Pardon and Its Effect on Civil Disabilities and Disqualifications
key_dimensions: A full Pardon completely wipes out conviction — restores convict to position as if never convicted
Remission, Commutation, Reprieve, Respite do NOT remove civil disqualifications — UPSC trap
Implications for electoral disqualifications under RPA, 1951 — does pardon remove bar on contesting elections?
Comparison with US pardon jurisprudence: full pardon vs. conditional pardon — Indian position

concepts.name: Pardoning Power and Separation of Powers Doctrine
key_dimensions: Pardoning power as an executive encroachment on judicial function — constitutional design rationale
Constituent Assembly debates: why pardoning power was given to President rather than judiciary
Balance between judicial finality and executive clemency as a check — constitutional philosophy
Contrast with UK (Royal Prerogative of Mercy) and USA (Article II, Section 2) — comparative dimension

concepts.name: Right of the Convict in Mercy Petition Process
key_dimensions: Is there a constitutional right to file a mercy petition? — not explicitly in Article 72, evolved through practice
SC mandates: copy of rejection must be communicated; convict must be given reasonable time after rejection before execution
Shatrughan Chauhan case: minimum 14 days' notice after rejection of mercy petition before execution
Whether convict has right to be personally heard by President — SC says NO, but must be heard through representation

concepts.name: Procedure for Disposal of Mercy Petitions — Ministry of Home Affairs Role
key_dimensions: Petition addressed to President but processed through Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)
MHA's role: seeks report from State government, examines case, makes recommendation to President via Cabinet
Constitutional gap: no statutory time limit for President to decide — criticism and reform suggestions
UPSC angle: President is bound by Cabinet recommendation but CAN send it back once — procedural nuance

concepts.name: Pardoning Power in Context of Scheduled Offences and Special Laws
key_dimensions: NDPS Act, TADA, POCSO — whether President's pardoning power extends to special statutes
Courts have held Article 72 has universal application — no law can curtail presidential pardoning power
COFEPOSA and preventive detention laws — whether pardoning power applies to preventive detention orders
Legislative attempts to restrict pardoning power — constitutionality and judicial response

concepts.name: Political Considerations and Abuse of Pardoning Power — Controversies
key_dimensions: Epuru Sudhakar case: SC explicitly held that political considerations (e.g., caste, religion) VITIATE the pardon
High-profile controversies: Rajiv Gandhi assassination convicts, Bilkis Bano case (remission by Gujarat Governor)
Distinction: Bilkis Bano involved Governor's Article 161 powers — often confused with President's Article 72
Democratic accountability: pardoning power as an executive act insulated from parliamentary scrutiny — gap

concepts.name: Pardoning Power vs. Suspension, Remission, and Commutation under CrPC/BNS
key_dimensions: Section 432-435 CrPC (now Section 473-478 BNSS): statutory power of State/Central government to remit/commute sentences
Critical distinction: CrPC/BNSS powers are STATUTORY and require consultation with presiding judge; Article 72 is CONSTITUTIONAL and independent
CrPC Section 435 (BNSS 476): Central government's concurrence needed for certain cases — interplay with Article 72
UPSC trap: Article 72 and CrPC/BNSS powers are separate, parallel streams — exercising one does not bar the other

concepts.name: Pardoning Power and Article 21 — Constitutional Safeguard Dimension
key_dimensions: Pardoning power as a safeguard against judicial error — constitutional safety valve for wrongful convictions
Article 21 right to life: how delay, solitary confinement on death row, and non-disposal of mercy petitions violate it
SC's evolution: from seeing pardon as grace/privilege to recognising convict's legitimate constitutional expectation
Interface with curative petition (last judicial remedy) and mercy petition — sequence and hierarchy of remedies
